lesson.title: Biometric categorisation and emotion recognition
lesson.summary: Separate biometric emotion inference from sensitive categorisation and check prohibitions first.

prerequisites.reason: The emotion-recognition definition depends on biometric data as its basis. The categorisation definition depends on biometric data as its basis.

blocks: **Emotion recognition** identifies or infers emotions or intentions from a person's biometric data. Inferring engagement from facial processing differs from reading an explicit questionnaire answer: the data and inference matter.
Northbridge must record what is inferred and from which processed signals. A product title such as 'wellbeing assistant' cannot establish or remove this definition.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(39), 3(40); Annex III 1(b), 1(c); Article 5(1)(f), 5(1)(g)

blocks: **Biometric categorisation** assigns people to categories using biometric data, subject to the definition's ancillary-service and objective technical-necessity limit. Both parts of that narrow exclusion need evidence.
A commercial service label alone cannot justify the exclusion. Ask which category is inferred, from which biometric data, and why the ancillary function is technically necessary.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(39), 3(40); Annex III 1(b), 1(c); Article 5(1)(f), 5(1)(g)

blocks: Annex III 1(b) concerns categorisation by sensitive or protected attributes inferred from biometric data; point 1(c) concerns emotion recognition. They are listed only insofar as their use is otherwise legally permitted.
Article 5 can prohibit specific emotion settings or sensitive-category inference. High-risk treatment does not make those uses lawful. The later prohibition module examines each exact boundary.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(39), 3(40); Annex III 1(b), 1(c); Article 5(1)(f), 5(1)(g)

blocks: Fictional case: Northbridge considers two tools—one infers intentions from facial signals, another infers a sensitive category from those signals. Keep their purposes distinct and check each relevant rule.
An emotion system is not defined by categorising a person into any group; a categorisation system is not automatically emotion recognition. Do not collapse the definitions into 'all cameras'.

options.reason: Article 3(39) includes emotion or intention inference from biometrics.
